hints: Picture the six carbon atoms of benzene joined in a ring and think what regular polygon and bond angle would keep all C-C bonds identical and strain free.
Recall how many sigma bonds each carbon makes in benzene (two to C plus one to H) and what hybridisation gives three planar orbitals.
Think about what orbitals are left over on each carbon after sigma bonding and how they can overlap above and below the ring.
walkthrough:
Fix the shape and angle**
Imagine six identical $\text{C-C}$ bonds in a flat ring. The only regular shape that fits is a regular hexagon, which is completely planar. Each interior angle is $120^{\circ}$, so every $\text{C-C-C}$ bond angle is $120^{\circ}$. This flat shape lets all the p orbitals line up in parallel.

Work out the hybridisation**
Each carbon in benzene bonds to two other carbons and one hydrogen, that is three sigma bond regions with no lone pair. That is the classic trigonal planar set, so each carbon is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised. The three $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals lie in the plane at $120^{\circ}$ to each other.

Build sigma then pi**
The $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals meet head on, end-on-end, between neighbouring carbons and between carbon and hydrogen. That head on overlap makes the strong $\sigma$ framework. Each carbon still has one unhybridised p orbital sticking up and down perpendicular to the ring. These six p orbitals overlap sideways with neighbours on both sides, merging into a continuous delocalised $\pi$ cloud above and below the ring.

Final answer: Bond angle $120^{\circ}$, planar regular hexagonal ring.
Carbons are $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised.
$\text{sp}^2$ orbitals overlap end-on to form $\sigma$ bonds, unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways above and below ring to form delocalised $\pi$ system.

hints: Remember $\text{AlCl}_3$ is an electron pair acceptor, so think how it can pull $\text{Cl}^{-}$ from $\text{Cl}_2$ to leave a positive chlorine species.
walkthrough:
Make the chloronium electrophile**
$\text{AlCl}_3$ acts as a Lewis acid. It accepts $\text{Cl}^{-}$ from $\text{Cl}_2$. That heterolytic split leaves $\text{Cl}^{+}$, the strong electrophile that will attack benzene, and $\text{AlCl}_4^{-}$. Write the balanced ionic equation as $$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cl}^{+} + \text{AlCl}_4^{-}$$

hints: Start from the delocalised pi cloud of benzene acting as nucleophile toward $\text{Cl}^{+}$ and think where the first curly arrow must come from.
Picture the temporary loss of aromaticity when $\text{Cl}$ bonds to one carbon, consider where the positive charge sits and that the C-H on that carbon is still present.
Think how aromaticity is restored by removing that same hydrogen as $\text{H}^{+}$ and where the electrons of the C-H bond must go.
walkthrough:
Attack by the ring**
The benzene pi cloud is electron rich. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the $\text{Cl}^{+}$ electrophile. This forms a new $\text{C-Cl}$ bond and breaks the aromaticity temporarily.

Draw the arenium ion**
The carbon that gains $\text{Cl}$ becomes $\text{sp}^3$ and still carries its H, so show $\text{C(H)(Cl)}$. The positive charge is now delocalised over the remaining five carbons of the ring. This is the Wheland or arenium intermediate. Keep the charge inside the ring structure.

Restore aromaticity**
A base, often $\text{AlCl}_4^{-}$, removes the hydrogen from that same carbon. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond back into the ring to reform the pi system, releasing $\text{H}^{+}$. The ring becomes aromatic chlorobenzene again.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene $\pi$ system to $\text{Cl}^{+}$; Wheland intermediate with $\text{Cl}$ and H on same $\text{sp}^3$ carbon and + charge delocalised in ring; curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to give $\text{H}^{+}$ and chlorobenzene.

hints: Look at what replaces a ring H in Fig. 5.4, an acyl group $\text{RCO}$ using an acyl chloride with $\text{AlCl}_3$, and recall the family of benzene substitution reactions.
walkthrough:
Name the ring reaction**
Chlorobenzene keeps its aromatic ring but gains a $\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$ group in place of H, using $\text{ClCOCH}_2\text{Cl}$ and $\text{AlCl}_3$. That is acylation of the ring by an electrophile, so the mechanism type is electrophilic substitution.
Final answer: Electrophilic substitution (Friedel-Crafts acylation).

hints: Compound Q in Fig. 5.4 is the 2-substituted product, so think where else the new acyl group could enter relative to the Cl atom on chlorobenzene.
walkthrough:
Place the acyl group elsewhere**
Q shows the $\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$ group ortho to the ring Cl, that is 2-substituted. The same electrophile can attack at the para position to give the 4-substituted isomer, $\text{4-Cl-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$, or at the meta position to give the 3-substituted isomer. Draw the benzene with Cl and $\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{Cl}$ in 1,4 or 1,3 positions.
Final answer: 4-chloro isomer: $\text{Cl-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO-CH}_2\text{-Cl}$ with $\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$ para to Cl (3-substituted isomer also allowed).

hints: Rank the three C-Cl types by how easily water attacks, recalling that acyl chlorides fume in moist air while chlorobenzene needs harsh conditions.
Compare the carbon attached to Cl, how many electronegative atoms pull electrons away in $\text{RCOCl}$ versus $\text{RCl}$.
Think why the C-Cl bond in chlorobenzene has partial double bond character through overlap of the Cl lone pair with the ring pi system.
walkthrough:
State the order**
From fuming instantly to no reaction with water, the order is acyl chloride easiest, then alkyl chloride, then aryl chloride hardest: $$\text{RCOCl} > \text{RCl} > \text{ArCl}$$

Explain acyl most reactive**
In $\text{R-C(=O)-Cl}$ the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two electronegative atoms, O and Cl. It carries a large $\delta+$ and is wide open to nucleophilic attack by water. The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is also weakened and breaks easily.

Contrast alkyl and aryl**
In an alkyl chloride $\text{R-Cl}$ the carbon is bonded to only one electronegative atom, so $\delta+$ is smaller. Alkyl groups also push electrons by positive inductive effect, strengthening the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond a little. In an aryl chloride the Cl lone pair overlaps with the ring pi system, giving the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character. That makes it much stronger and blocks nucleophilic attack, so chlorobenzene does not hydrolyse under normal conditions.

Final answer: Easiest acyl chloride > alkyl chloride > aryl chloride hardest.
Acyl C is most $\delta+$ attached to O and Cl, C-Cl weakest, easily attacked by nucleophiles.
Alkyl C is less $\delta+$ attached to one Cl only, strengthened by alkyl electron donation.
Aryl C-Cl has partial double bond character from Cl lone pair delocalisation into ring, strongest, resists hydrolysis.

hints: Compare Q with tulobuterol, identify which C-Cl is replaced by $\text{NHC(CH}_3)_3$ and which $\text{C=O}$ becomes $\text{CH-OH}$.
Recall what type of amine reagent substitutes an alkyl chloride and what hydride reagent reduces a ketone without touching the aryl chloride.
If substitution happens first the intermediate Z still contains the ketone, think what its structure $\text{Ar-CO-CH}_2\text{-NHC(CH}_3)_3$ looks like.
walkthrough:
Spot the two changes**
Q is $\text{Ar-CO-CH}_2\text{-Cl}$. Tulobuterol is $\text{Ar-CH(OH)-CH}_2\text{-NH-C(CH}_3)_3$. So the $\text{CH}_2\text{-Cl}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2\text{-NH-C(CH}_3)_3$ by substitution, and the $\text{C=O}$ becomes $\text{CH-OH}$ by reduction. The aryl Cl is untouched throughout.

Choose the reagents**
For step 3 use tert-butylamine, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CNH}_2$, in ethanol to do nucleophilic substitution at the alkyl chloride. For step 4 use $\text{LiAlH}_4$ or $\text{NaBH}_4$ to reduce the ketone to a secondary alcohol. Either order works, but substitution first is simplest.

Draw Z**
If substitution is step 3, Z is the amino-ketone: benzene with ortho Cl, plus $\text{-C(=O)-CH}_2\text{-NH-C(CH}_3)_3$ side chain. That is $\text{2-Cl-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_2\text{NHC(CH}_3)_3$. Step 4 then reduces $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH(OH)}$ to give tulobuterol.

Final answer: Step 3: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CNH}_2$ in ethanol, nucleophilic substitution of alkyl $\text{-CH}_2\text{-Cl}$.
Step 4: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ or $\text{NaBH}_4$, reduction of ketone to alcohol.
Z is $\text{2-Cl-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO-CH}_2\text{-NH-C(CH}_3)_3$ (amino-ketone).

hints: Think of left and right hands and how they relate to plane polarised light rotation.
walkthrough:
Define the pair**
Enantiomers are a pair of stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other but cannot be laid exactly on top of each other, just like left and right hands. They rotate plane polarised light by the same amount in opposite directions.
Final answer: Non-superimposable mirror images (that rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions).

hints: Consider that receptors in the body are chiral, so what happens if only one mirror image fits well and the mixture contains 50 percent of each.
walkthrough:
Link to drug action**
Body receptors are chiral, so often only one enantiomer gives the wanted effect while the other is less active or has side effects. Making a racemic mixture therefore wastes half the product and forces a difficult separation to get the pure active drug.
Final answer: Need to separate isomers as only one enantiomer has desired biological activity / other may be inactive or harmful, halving effective yield.

hints: Think what kind of catalyst could favour attack from one face of a planar carbonyl to create one handed alcohol selectively.
walkthrough:
Control the handedness**
To make a single enantiomer, carry out the key bond forming step in a chiral environment. A chiral catalyst or a specific enzyme directs attack to one face only, producing mainly one optical isomer.
Final answer: Use a chiral catalyst or enzyme.

hints: Count unique carbons in tulobuterol, remembering the three methyl carbons on $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$ are identical and the benzene has six different carbons due to ortho substitution.
walkthrough:
Count distinct carbons**
Tulobuterol has: 6 different ring carbons because 1,2-disubstitution makes all ring positions unique, plus $\text{CH(OH)}$, plus $\text{CH}_2$, plus quaternary $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$, plus one type for the three equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups. That is $6+1+1+1+1 = 10$ signals in the $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum.
Final answer: 10 peaks.

hints: In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ the $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NH}$ protons exchange away, so focus only on C-H protons and use Table 5.1 to match shift ranges.
Identify the 9 equivalent methyl protons and predict their shift and splitting when they have no neighbouring protons.
For the benzylic $\text{CH}$ and the four aromatic protons, use the n+1 rule with neighbours to predict triplet versus multiplet and count hydrogens.
walkthrough:
Remove exchangeable protons**
Dissolving in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ shakes away $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NH}$ signals. You are left with only carbon bound protons: the tert-butyl $9\text{H}$, the $\text{CH}_2\text{N}$ given as doublet, the benzylic $\text{CH}$, and the four aromatic H. That gives four proton environments in total.

Assign the tert-butyl singlet**
The nine $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$ protons are all equivalent alkane protons, $\delta = 0.9-1.7$. With no protons on the adjacent quaternary carbon, $n=0$ so $n+1 = 1$, a singlet integrating to $9\text{H}$.

Assign the benzylic CH and aromatic H**
The $\text{Ar-CH(OH)-}$ proton is alkyl next to aromatic ring and next to electronegative O, $\delta = 2.3-3.0$ to $3.2-4.0$. It couples to the neighbouring $\text{CH}_2$ ($2\text{H}$), so $n+1 = 3$, a triplet integrating to $1\text{H}$. The four ring protons are $\text{H-Ar}$, $\delta = 6.0-9.0$, splitting each other into a complex multiplet integrating to $4\text{H}$.

Final answer: $\delta$ 0.9-1.7, 9H, singlet, $\text{-CH}_3$ / alkane $(\text{C(CH}_3)_3)$.
$\delta$ 2.3-3.0 or 3.2-4.0, 1H, triplet, $\text{Ar-CH}$ / alkyl next to electronegative atom $(\text{CH-OH})$.
$\delta$ 6.0-9.0, 4H, multiplet, $\text{H-Ar}$ / aromatic.
